newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. expects "completely free" Mexico vote - envoy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expects "completely free" Mexico vote - envoy.

text.p: James Jones, the departing U.S. ambassador to Mexico, said on Monday that Washington expected Mexican elections next month to be "completely free."

Giving a final news conference before leaving his post after almost four years, Jones said a historic opposition victory in the July 6 vote would not change U.S. policy or alter investors' opinions about Mexico.
"I have great confidence in the credibility of the elections," he said.
"The only interest which we have in the United States is that in these elections democracy progresses and we are sure that will happen," he said.
Polls showed President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled Mexico for 68 unbroken years, may lose its lower house majority in Congress for the first time.
A left-wing veteran, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, also was likely to become the first elected mayor of Mexico City in modern history and the opposition might gain a couple of governorships in key states.
This has led to speculation that markets might react badly but Jones said he saw no big problems with an opposition win.
"I don't see that either the financial community or the political leadership of the United States would think that there would be a reason to change our relationship with Mexico," he said.
Leaders of Mexico's main political parties shared "similar values to those we have in the United States," he added.
Jones also defended the Republican Gov. William Weld of Massachusetts as a suitable replacement for him in the sensitive Mexico embassy post.
President Bill Clinton wants Weld for the job but some members of Congress, including the influential Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, have objected.
Helms has said Weld is "a little loose with his lips" and not "ambassador quality material" but Jones disputed this.
"Governor Weld has the qualities for this post," Jones said. "I respect the position of Senator Helms but I don't agree with it."
The departing ambassador also praised Zedillo's reforms over the past 2 1/2 years, saying they created a "positive atmosphere" in Mexico for foreign investment.
Jones was to return to the United States next week to become president of the international division of Warnaco, an American underwear manufacturer.
